ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory disease limited to the colon and rectum, causing continuous mucosal ulceration and bloody diarrhoea. Diagnosis relies on endoscopy and histology; severity guides treatment and surveillance for cancer.

sections.p: UC is a continuous inflammation of the colonic mucosa starting in the rectum and extending proximally. Diagnosis requires colonoscopy with biopsies showing crypt architectural distortion and inflammatory infiltrates.
b: Continuous colonic involvement, never skips segments
Biopsies rule out infection and confirm chronic inflammation

t.b: Does the colon show continuous mucosal ulceration and histologic features of chronic colitis? Positive findings confirm UC; normal mucosa makes diagnosis unlikely.
Is an infectious cause present? Positive results redirect treatment to antibiotics, not immunosuppression.
Is there intestinal inflammation? Elevated levels support IBD; low levels suggest functional disease.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the Mayo Clinic score (stool frequency, rectal bleeding, endoscopic appearance, physician’s global assessment) and by extent (proctitis, left‑sided, extensive).
b: Mild: <4 stools/day, no systemic signs
Moderate: >4 stools/day, some bleeding, anemia
Severe: >6 stools/day, fever, tachycardia, anemia

sections.p: Exact cause is unknown; a dysregulated immune response to gut flora in genetically susceptible individuals is primary. In low‑resource settings, consider co‑existing infections that can mimic or trigger flares.
b: Genetic susceptibility (e.g., HLA‑DRB1*01)
Abnormal mucosal immune response to microbiota
Environmental triggers: smoking cessation, diet, antibiotics
Infections that can aggravate disease: CMV, C. difficile, TB colitis

sections.p: Patients present with bloody diarrhoea, urgency, tenesmus, and abdominal cramping. Systemic features (weight loss, fatigue) appear with moderate‑severe disease.
b: Bloody, mucus‑laden stools
Rectal urgency and tenesmus
Abdominal pain, usually left‑sided

sections.p: Investigations confirm diagnosis, assess severity, and exclude mimics. When a test is unavailable, use clinical scoring and basic labs.
b: Baseline CBC, CRP, ESR for inflammation
Liver function tests before thiopurines

t.b: Is there anemia or leukocytosis? Anemia supports chronic blood loss; leukocytosis may indicate severe inflammation.
Is systemic inflammation present? Elevated values correlate with disease activity.
Is there colonic dilation suggesting toxic megacolon? Dilatation >6 cm warrants urgent surgery.

sections.p: Complications include toxic megacolon, severe hemorrhage, perforation, and colorectal cancer. Recognize early to prevent mortality.
b: Toxic megacolon: distended abdomen, fever, tachycardia
Massive rectal bleeding
Perforation with peritonitis

sections.p: Treat active inflammation, maintain remission, and monitor for cancer. Choose drugs based on severity and safety profile; avoid unnecessary steroids in mild disease.
b: 5‑ASA (mesalamine) for mild‑moderate disease – topical for proctitis, oral for extensive disease
Corticosteroids for moderate‑severe flares – rapid control, taper quickly
Immunomodulators (azathioprine, 6‑MP) for steroid‑sparing maintenance
Biologics (anti‑TNF, vedolizumab, ustekinumab) for refractory disease

sections.p: Regular colonoscopic surveillance begins 8‑10 years after diagnosis to detect dysplasia. Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus; counsel on smoking cessation and nutrition.
b: Surveillance colonoscopy every 1–3 years after 8 years of disease
Bone density monitoring if long‑term steroids used

sections.p: Conditions that can mimic UC include infectious colitis, Crohn’s disease, ischemic colitis, and radiation proctitis.
b: Crohn’s disease – skip lesions, transmural inflammation
Infectious colitis – acute onset, pathogen identified
Ischemic colitis – segmental, often in elderly

sections.p: Normal fecal calprotectin does not exclude mild UC; histology may appear normal in early disease; C. difficile toxin can be false‑negative.
b: Low calprotectin in early or mild disease
Biopsies taken from healed segments may miss active inflammation
Negative stool PCR does not rule out CMV colitis in immunosuppressed patients

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with distension
Profuse rectal bleeding or drop in hemoglobin

faq.q: Why does UC always involve the rectum?
faq.a: The rectal mucosa is the first site exposed to fecal antigens, and the disease spreads proximally in a continuous pattern.

faq.q: Can UC become a full‑thickness disease?
faq.a: UC is limited to mucosa and submucosa; transmural involvement suggests Crohn’s disease or complications like toxic megacolon.

faq.q: Is colon cancer common in UC?
faq.a: Risk rises after 8–10 years of extensive disease; regular surveillance colonoscopy reduces mortality.

exam: Describe the endoscopic and histologic criteria that differentiate ulcerative colitis from Crohn’s disease.
Explain how the Mayo Clinic score is used to grade disease severity and guide therapy.
List the surveillance strategy for colorectal cancer in a patient with 12 years of extensive ulcerative colitis.
